_readme: Curation layer for Jonah chapter 1. Everything else is derived by
Generated from scripts/build-jonah-glossary.mjs — edit the table there, not
this file, so the judgement stays in one reviewable place.
NEEDS SPECIALIST REVIEW. Glosses are short teaching meanings chosen for a
beginner reading Jonah, not lexicon entries. Hand-supplied roots are the
least certain content here and should be checked first.
Roots are deliberately WITHHELD from פָּנִים, עִיר, אֵת and מַלָּח even
though Strong's offers derivations, because those derivations are guesses.

words.notes: The divine name. Hebrew manuscripts point it with the vowels of אֲדֹנָי “Lord”, which is what is read aloud; JPS renders it “the LORD” in small capitals.
Untranslatable: it marks a definite direct object rather than meaning anything itself. Strong's derives it from אוֹת “sign”, which is not correct — see the family note.
Plural in form, singular in sense. Strong's files it under פנה “to turn”; that is an etymological guess, so no root is highlighted here.
Plural in form. Used of the God of Israel with singular verbs, and of other gods with plural ones — Jonah 1:5 has the sailors crying to their own אֱלֹהִים.
Jonah goes down repeatedly in this chapter — down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into its hold — and in 2:6 down to the roots of the mountains.
Literally a pebble, from the practice of casting stones to decide a matter — Jonah 1:7.
An adjective, not the verb. Jonah 1:9: “I am a Hebrew, and I fear (יָרֵא) the LORD” — same consonants as H3372, different word class.

words.familyNotes: The noun סַעַר and the verb סָעַר both appear in Jonah 1 — the sea storms, and there is a storm.

words.gloss: to be calm, to grow quiet

words.notes: Overlaps with יָלַךְ (H3212); the two share a paradigm between them, הָלַךְ supplying some forms and יָלַךְ others.
Used with commands, where לֹא negates statements. Jonah 1:14: “let us not perish”.

words.familyNotes: One of the clearest root families in Hebrew: דָּבָר a word, דִּבֶּר to speak, מִדְבָּר wilderness (disputed).

words.notes: Strong's derives it from עוּר “to awake”, glossing a city as “a place guarded by waking”. That is folk etymology, so no root is marked.

words.familyNotes: One word covers wind, breath and spirit. Jonah 1:4 has the LORD hurling a great רוּחַ onto the sea — wind, plainly, but the same word carries the other senses elsewhere.

words.notes: Related to מֶלַח “salt” — a salt-water man. Not marked as a root here, since the connection is a plausible guess rather than a paradigm.
Very general: any made object. In Jonah 1:5 it is the ship's cargo and tackle, thrown overboard.
In Jonah 1:5 the sailors lighten the ship by throwing the cargo out.
Occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. Jonah is asleep in its יַרְכְּתֵי — its innermost part.
רַב הַחֹבֵל in Jonah 1:6 is “the chief of the sailors” — the captain.
Rare and uncertain. Jonah 1:6: “perhaps God will give thought to us”.
A longer, weightier alternative to אֲנִי. Jonah uses it in 1:9 to answer who he is.
Dual in form, like several natural pairs in Hebrew.
Jonah 1:13: the men “dug” to bring the ship back to land — Hebrew for rowing hard against a sea.

words.familyNotes: Not “soul” in the later philosophical sense: נֶפֶשׁ is the living, breathing self. Jonah 1:14 asks not to perish for this man's נֶפֶשׁ — his life.

words.notes: דָּם נָקִי “innocent blood” in Jonah 1:14 is a fixed legal phrase for unpunished killing.

words.familyNotes: Verb and noun together in Jonah 1:16: וַיִּזְבְּחוּ זֶבַח — “they sacrificed a sacrifice”. Hebrew does this often, and it is not redundancy but emphasis.
The same pairing as זבח, in the same verse: וַיִּדְּרוּ נְדָרִים — “they vowed vows”.

words.notes: The same word as דָּג in a feminine form. Jonah 2:2 uses the masculine, 2:1 the feminine, for the same creature.
Plural in form. Used for the seat of feeling as well as the physical gut — Jonah prays from the מֵעֵי of the fish.
The realm of the dead. Not 'hell' in the later sense — Sheol is where everyone goes, without moral sorting.
In Hebrew the heart is where thinking and deciding happen, not primarily feeling.
Also means a spring of water — the same word, from the shape of the opening.
One word for both, because a temple is a god's palace.
Dual in form, like שָׁמַיִם — Hebrew treats water as inherently plural.
The same word as in יַם־סוּף, the Sea of Reeds.
Jonah 2:7: the earth's bars closed behind him — the underworld imagined as a barred gate.
Not 'eternity' in the abstract; it means a horizon so distant it cannot be seen past.
Literally a breath or vapour. The keyword of Ecclesiastes, used here of worthless idols.
Hard to translate: covenant loyalty and kindness together. Often rendered lovingkindness or steadfast love.
The noun behind the name Joshua, and behind Jesus.
Also a way of living — 'their evil way' in Jonah 3:10 is conduct, not a road.
Jonah's whole message is one word of this verb — נֶהְפָּכֶת, 'is being overthrown'.
The root behind אָמֵן — to be firm, to rely on.
Coarse cloth worn in mourning. Jonah 3:8 puts it on the cattle too.

words.familyNotes: The verb טָעַם means to taste; the noun means both a taste and a considered decision. Jonah 3:7 has the king's טַעַם — his decree — and 3:7 also forbids anyone to taste (טָעַם) anything.

words.notes: Related to אֲדָמָה, the ground — the human is the earth-creature.
Same consonants as רַע 'evil' and רֵעַ 'companion' but a different word. Unpointed Hebrew cannot tell them apart; context and vowels can.
Turning back physically and turning from wrongdoing are the same verb — the pivot of the whole book.
The same verb means to comfort and to change one's mind. Jonah 3:10: God relented of the evil he had said he would do.
The same word for nose and for anger — from the flaring of the nostrils. אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, 'long of nose', means slow to anger.

words.gloss: to do well, to be good

words.notes: The sirocco off the desert — dry, scorching, and in Jonah 4:8 sent deliberately.
Four times in the book God 'appoints' something: the fish, the gourd, the worm and the wind.
The plant is unidentified. Strong's guesses the castor-oil plant; the text only says it grew fast and died faster.

words.familyNotes: The same root as יַבָּשָׁה, dry land, in chapter 1 — a plant withers by the same word the sea does not cover.

words.notes: The book's last word turns on it: should God not pity Nineveh?
Jonah 4:11: Nineveh's people cannot tell right hand from left — either children, or moral ignorance, or both.
Related to אָדָם, the human — the creature made from it.
אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם — 'long of nostrils', i.e. slow to anger. Jonah quotes the formula at God as a complaint.

words.gloss: to be evil, to do harm

words.notes: Same root as שָׁלוֹם: to make whole, hence to pay what is owed. Jonah 2:10 — “what I have vowed I will pay”.
